strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First closed-form optimal transforms for weight-activation quantization with explicit construction and optimality guarantees (Theorem 1)
Rigorous mathematical analysis: Clean two-step proof strategy with separate treatments for FP and INT formats; proofs appear sound and comprehensive
Theoretical insight explaining empirical success: Demonstrates that Hadamard is the only data-agnostic component in the optimal formulation, providing principled justification for its effectiveness
Practical efficiency: Closed-form solution requiring only Cholesky+SVD, more computationally efficient than learning-based alternatives (SpinQuant, FlatQuant)
Broad format coverage: Addresses both emerging FP formats (MXFP, NVFP) and traditional INT formats
Consistent experimental improvements: Layer-wise quantization loss reduction across all formats (Table 1) and consistent accuracy gains on LLM benchmarks (Table 2)
weaknesses: Multiple unvalidated theoretical approximations: (1) First-order approximation in Eq. 7 drops cross-term without quantifying impact, (2) block-wise independence assumption lacks justification, (3) smooth error models are approximations not empirically validated against real quantization behavior
Loose INT optimality bounds: Only d^o(1) or d-factor optimal for INT case—for typical block size d=128, this represents a substantial gap from true optimality

Limited and preliminary experimental validation: Paper explicitly labels experiments as 'preliminary'; lacks comparison with other data-aware methods (SpinQuant, FlatQuant); only evaluates RTN+AbsMax scaling; no GPTQ integration; marginal NVFP4 improvements

Unresolved practical deployment challenges: Per-block transforms complicate kernel fusion; inference-time cost not analyzed; storage overhead not discussed; damping parameter λ selection not explained; no ablation on critical hyperparameters

Missing ablation studies: No sensitivity analysis for damping parameter λ; no investigation of when WUSH significantly outperforms Hadamard vs. when gains are marginal; similar WUSH vs. WUS performance for NVFP4 unexplored

Modest end-to-end accuracy improvements: While layer losses improve substantially, end-to-end accuracy gains are smaller (e.g., Qwen3-8B MXFP4: +2.8% absolute recovery); NVFP4 improvements often within noise margins
FP theory-practice mismatch: Section 2.2.3 proves orthogonal transforms should not help in ideal FP, yet Hadamard helps empirically for MXFP4; explanation as 'hybrid behavior' lacks rigor
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned; missing implementation details (Hadamard normalization, rank-deficiency handling); calibration overhead not measured
Limited experimental scope: Only 32 calibration samples tested; limited model diversity (mainly Qwen/Llama); no statistical significance testing despite visible variance in results

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: Derives closed-form optimal transforms (Theorem 1) with complete proofs for both FP and INT quantizers, providing theoretical justification for empirical success of Hadamard transforms

Addresses fundamental question with principled approach: Explains why data-agnostic Hadamard transforms work well by deriving their optimality from first principles, filling a theoretical gap in prior work

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across multiple models (Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen 8B/14B/32B) and formats (NVFP4, MXFP4, INT4), with substantial per-layer loss reductions (Table 1)
Practical efficiency: GPU kernel implementation with only 1.3% overhead vs optimized Hadamard baselines; achieves 6.6× speedup over BF16 while maintaining competitive accuracy
Natural integration with GPTQ: Algorithm 1 elegantly decomposes and interleaves GPTQ error propagation with transform construction, demonstrating practical applicability
Clear presentation and intuitive visualizations: Excellent Figure 1 showing geometric intuition; well-structured derivations with clear delineation between assumptions, approximations, and results
weaknesses: Gap between theoretical guarantees and practice: For INT quantizers, optimality is only guaranteed within d^o(1) factor for tail-bounded distributions and d factor for general distributions (Eq. 30); paper lacks clear guidance on when these gaps matter practically

Modest improvements in several settings: NVFP4 gains are marginal (~0.26 points), potentially within run-to-run variance; Figure 3 shows overlapping error bars; WUS (without Hadamard) performs nearly identically for NVFP4, questioning Hadamard's necessity in some cases

Theoretical assumptions may not hold in practice: Unbiased quantization assumption doesn't account for clipping; i.i.d. column assumption for probabilistic reformulation is a modeling choice; first-order approximation (Eq. 13) lacks explicit error bounds

Limited scope: Only evaluated on 4-bit W4A4 quantization without analysis of scaling to other bitwidths (2-bit, 8-bit); limited to transformer-based LLMs without evaluation on other architectures or domains

Incomplete experimental analysis: Missing ablations on damping ratio λ, sensitivity to calibration data size/quality, and block size effects; no quantified computational cost of SVD-based calibration; limited failure case analysis
Calibration cost not addressed: SVD computation required for each block per layer; memory overhead for storing per-block transforms not discussed; actual wall-clock calibration time not provided

Missing implementation details: Hyperparameter choices not well justified; no mention of code release (critical for reproducibility); some experimental details relegated to appendix; GPU kernel design rationale could be clearer
